newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's central bank head sees rosy economy.
newsitem.headline: Canada's central bank head sees rosy economy.

text.p: The governor of Canada's central bank painted a sunny picture of the Canadian economy on Tuesday, predicting more jobs, strong economic growth and a stronger dollar and stocks this year and next.
"The basic foundations of our economy look much healthier thay they have in much of the last 20 years," Bank of Governor Gordon Thiessen told the Senate banking community.
"We're going through a major transformation in this country," the central banker said. "I think we're through the worst part of it."

He said inflation would likely remain in the lower half of the bank's targeted one to three percent. But he added that Canada's consumer price index, a major indicator of inflation, was probably overstated by half a percentage point each year.
The latest figures showed a 2.2 percent annual rise in the overall Canadian CPI and a 1.8 percent rise if food and energy were excluded.
Low inflation went hand in hand with the Bank of Canada's moves to sustain low interest rates, now at their lowest level since 1961, Thiessen said.
He predicted that the impact of rate cuts would kick in this year to boost employment, increase consumer spending and push production closer to full capacity.

"The prospects are good for reducing much of the present slack in our economy over the course of 1997 and 1998 and for a substantial improvement in the employment situation," Thiessen told the committee.
Unemployment in Canada has hovered for months just below a stubbornly high 10 percent. But Thiessen said job growth normally lagged economic expansion and was expected to pick up this year.
He pointed to the creation of 220,000 jobs in the private sector last year as a sign of things to come.
"I'm not suggesting it will happen as quickly as we all might like," he added.
Thiessen also repeated his prediction that Canadian gross domestic product would rise four percent in 1997.

He said he expected the Canadian dollar to appreciate against the U.S. dollar in the long term, as Canada improved its current account and benefited from a stable political environment and rising commodity prices.
The Canadian dollar has weakened in recent weeks amid worries about about a possible U.S. interest rate hike at a time when Canadian rates are flat or falling.
A widening spread between U.S. and Canadian rates could lure capital away from Canada into the United States, further weakening the local currency, now trading below 73 U.S. cents.
Thiessen said Canada's improved finances gave the central bank more room to maneuver in response to any U.S. rate hikes.
He was also optimistic about prospects for Canadian stocks, which rallied last year but have slumped lately.
"I think there's no doubt that the outlook for Canada for an expanding economy does leave room for some optimism in the stock markets," he said.
